title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false-positive failure in an automated licence-plate reader, and it happened at the point where a system alert turns into police action. The reader misread the first letter of a plate and matched a BMW to a similar stolen vehicle, and the resulting alert was acted on as though it identified a stolen car. The failure mode is a system deployed without a human check at the moment of enforcement: an automated hit was treated as sufficient grounds for a stop rather than as a lead requiring confirmation.

Catching it would have required exactly what Flock says should happen, independent verification of the alert before enforcement. A check of the plate against the vehicle in front of the deputy, or of the full plate rather than the misread character, would have broken the chain between the bad read and the armed stop. The gap is not in the reading alone but in the absence of any step between the alert and the drawn weapon.

What is not established is that the tinted plate cover caused the misread, which is the sheriff's account rather than a finding, and that the deputy's actions were reasonable, which is the sheriff's characterisation rather than an independent conclusion.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was reportedly held at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff's office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction, called the deputy's actions reasonable, and Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
